newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST - HK Newspaper Editorials - June 16.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - HK Newspaper Editorials - June 16.

text.p: There are 15 days to go before the British colony reverts to China. These are highlights of comments in the Hong Kong press. The views expressed are those of the newspapers quoted and do not represent an editorial viewpoint of Reuters.

-- The ECONOMIC JOURNAL said localisation was a major reform aimed at enabling Hong Kong to be ruled by its own people. Under the colonial civil service system, expatriate civil servants enjoyed priviledges while Chinese were discriminated against, which now should be changed. The paper said some expatriate civil servants went too far by demanding an apology from the government because parts of its localisation plan were considered against human rights laws. Looking back on history in the past century, expatriate civil servants should appologise to their Chinese colleagues, not the other way round, it said.

-- The Beijing-funded TA KUNG PAO said it was obvious that even after the handover some people would continue to create trouble. But if the Special Administrative Region government can do its job well, carry out the "one country, two systems" policy, maintain Hong Kong's stability and prosperity and safeguard people's rights and freedom, then all countries will want to develop good relations with Hong Kong without the territory going out of its way to please them.

-- APPLE DAILY said the comments of the former chief of Xinhau News Agency in Hong Kong, Xu Jiatun, showed that the 82-year-old still cared about China and remained loyal to the Communist Party. It said Xinhua News Agency should explain to Hong Kong people how the Communist Party would exist in the territory after the handover, otherwise many people would suspect that the Agency would become an overlord over the Chief Executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa.

-- The English-language HONGKONG STANDARD said it had becoming increasingly obvious recently that some potential Hong Kong candidates for the Queen's honours list might have declined their awards, seeing them as colonial relics. But there was certainly nothing wrong with the idea of rewarding local people who had contributed either to the China's reunification or to Hong Kong's prosperity and stability.
